case_info.scenario: A 13-year-old male individual was referred to the ocular oncology service for evaluation of an optic nerve mass in the left eye. He reported decreased central vision in the left eye over the previous 2 to 3 weeks associated with mild conjunctival hyperemia and occasional eye pain. Peripheral vision was subjectively intact. He had no relevant medical history, no recent changes in health, no recent history of travel outside the country, and no family history of childhood cancer. Examination revealed an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/25 in the right eye and counting fingers at 2 ft in the left eye without improvement on pinhole, normal intraocular pressures, and unremarkable anterior segment findings in both eyes. In the left eye, there was an afferent pupillary defect, a few vitreous cells that did not limit the view of the retina or optic nerve, and a fluffy-appearing, white, elevated optic nerve lesion associated with a small peripapillary hemorrhage, peripapillary subretinal fluid extending into the macula and inferiorly, and scattered white lesions in the inferior retinal periphery (Figure 1). Examination of the right eye was unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion involving the left optic disc 1.9 mm in height associated with subretinal fluid and symmetric retrobulbar optic nerve size bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits showed a 3-mm enhancing nodule of the left optic disc but was otherwise unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Clinical case]
A 13-year-old male individual was referred to the ocular oncology service for evaluation of an optic nerve mass in the left eye. He reported decreased central vision in the left eye over the previous 2 to 3 weeks associated with mild conjunctival hyperemia and occasional eye pain. Peripheral vision was subjectively intact. He had no relevant medical history, no recent changes in health, no recent history of travel outside the country, and no family history of childhood cancer. Examination revealed an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/25 in the right eye and counting fingers at 2 ft in the left eye without improvement on pinhole, normal intraocular pressures, and unremarkable anterior segment findings in both eyes. In the left eye, there was an afferent pupillary defect, a few vitreous cells that did not limit the view of the retina or optic nerve, and a fluffy-appearing, white, elevated optic nerve lesion associated with a small peripapillary hemorrhage, peripapillary subretinal fluid extending into the macula and inferiorly, and scattered white lesions in the inferior retinal periphery (Figure 1). Examination of the right eye was unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion involving the left optic disc 1.9 mm in height associated with subretinal fluid and symmetric retrobulbar optic nerve size bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits showed a 3-mm enhancing nodule of the left optic disc but was otherwise unremarkable.

[Doctor]: While I appreciate the importance of non-invasive tests, the clinical presentation here suggests a significant and urgent concern. The optic nerve mass, combined with the rapid change in vision and retinal findings, points more towards a potential neoplasm or severe infectious process. A vitreous sample allows us to obtain a direct source for diagnosis, which is essential given the potential for rapid deterioration. Delaying this step could postpone appropriate treatment, which we cannot afford in this case.

Could we first pursue serologic tests for common infectious etiologies like toxoplasmosis or Bartonella, which might offer a diagnosis without those risks and are often standard before invasive procedures?
[Doctor]: While I acknowledge the risks associated with vitreous sampling, the urgency of the clinical situation warrants it. The combination of optic nerve mass and the associated symptoms strongly suggests a serious underlying pathology that could escalate quickly. Serologic tests, while useful, may introduce delays that could compromise the patient's vision further. We need a timely and accurate diagnosis to guide our management, and a vitreous sample provides the most immediate and direct insight into the underlying cause.
[AI Assistant]: I understand the urgency, but a targeted serologic panel for Toxoplasma, Bartonella, and syphilis can be resulted within 24-48 hours, often faster than scheduling and processing a vitreous biopsy. Given the lesion's appearance and peripheral retinal lesions, an infectious cause is highly plausible. Could you clarify why the diagnostic yield of a rapid infectious workup is insufficient compared to an immediate invasive procedure with its attendant risks?

case_info.scenario: A 13-year-old male individual was referred to the ocular oncology service for evaluation of an optic nerve mass in the left eye. He reported decreased central vision in the left eye over the previous 2 to 3 weeks associated with mild conjunctival hyperemia and occasional eye pain. Peripheral vision was subjectively intact. Examination revealed an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/25 in the right eye and counting fingers at 2 ft in the left eye without improvement on pinhole, normal intraocular pressures, and unremarkable anterior segment findings in both eyes. In the left eye, there was an afferent pupillary defect, a few vitreous cells that did not limit the view of the retina or optic nerve, and a fluffy-appearing, white, elevated optic nerve lesion associated with a small peripapillary hemorrhage, peripapillary subretinal fluid extending into the macula and inferiorly, and scattered white lesions in the inferior retinal periphery (Figure 1). B-scan ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion involving the left optic disc 1.9 mm in height associated with subretinal fluid and symmetric retrobulbar optic nerve size bilaterally. case_info.explanation: A. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

A 13-year-old male individual was referred to the ocular oncology service for evaluation of an optic nerve mass in the left eye. He had no relevant medical history, no recent changes in health, no recent history of travel outside the country, and no family history of childhood cancer. Examination revealed an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/25 in the right eye and counting fingers at 2 ft in the left eye without improvement on pinhole, normal intraocular pressures, and unremarkable anterior segment findings in both eyes. In the left eye, there was an afferent pupillary defect, a few vitreous cells that did not limit the view of the retina or optic nerve, and a fluffy-appearing, white, elevated optic nerve lesion associated with a small peripapillary hemorrhage, peripapillary subretinal fluid extending into the macula and inferiorly, and scattered white lesions in the inferior retinal periphery (Figure 1). Examination of the right eye was unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion involving the left optic disc 1.9 mm in height associated with subretinal fluid and symmetric retrobulbar optic nerve size bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits showed a 3-mm enhancing nodule of the left optic disc but was otherwise unremarkable.

He reported decreased central vision in the left eye over the previous 2 to 3 weeks associated with mild conjunctival hyperemia and occasional eye pain. Peripheral vision was subjectively intact. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

B-scan ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion involving the left optic disc 1.9 mm in height associated with subretinal fluid and symmetric retrobulbar optic nerve size bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits showed a 3-mm enhancing nodule of the left optic disc but was otherwise unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two

            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A 13-year-old male individual was referred to the ocular oncology service for evaluation of an optic nerve mass in the left eye. He reported decreased central vision in the left eye over the previous 2 to 3 weeks associated with mild conjunctival hyperemia and occasional eye pain. Peripheral vision was subjectively intact. He had no relevant medical history, no recent changes in health, no recent history of travel outside the country, and no family history of childhood cancer. Examination revealed an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/25 in the right eye and counting fingers at 2 ft in the left eye without improvement on pinhole, normal intraocular pressures, and unremarkable anterior segment findings in both eyes. In the left eye, there was an afferent pupillary defect, a few vitreous cells that did not limit the view of the retina or optic nerve, and a fluffy-appearing, white, elevated optic nerve lesion associated with a small peripapillary hemorrhage, peripapillary subretinal fluid extending into the macula and inferiorly, and scattered white lesions in the inferior retinal periphery (Figure 1). Examination of the right eye was unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion involving the left optic disc 1.9 mm in height associated with subretinal fluid and symmetric retrobulbar optic nerve size bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits showed a 3-mm enhancing nodule of the left optic disc but was otherwise unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

Examination of the right eye was unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion involving the left optic disc 1.9 mm in height associated with subretinal fluid and symmetric retrobulbar optic nerve size bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits showed a 3-mm enhancing nodule of the left optic disc but was otherwise unremarkable.
